articles.title: NASA’s Curiosity rover found a ‘sea of polygons’ on Mars
articles.summary: NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover found a field of honeycomb terrain in a Martian valley, a texture that has previously pointed to signs of water.
articles.body: The latest discovery from NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover is a field of honeycomb-shaped polygons covering a Martian valley called Valle Grande. As Gizmodo reports, Curiosity has snapped pictures of the unusual terrain texture before, called polygonal fractures, each about 1.5 to 3 inches wide, but NASA says it’s previously only found them in small patches, “nothing on the scale discovered in Valle Grande.” Curiosity captured a 360-degree panorama of the “sea of polygons” on June 19th and 20th (Martian sols 4,930 and 4,931) that shows the texture spreading out in all directions. Project scientist Ashwin Vasavada says the Curiosity team “measured their shapes and chemistry carefully and are hopeful there are clues in the data as to how these features formed.” NASA says billions of years ago, “lakes and streams dappled the lower foothills of Mount Sharp, a 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain that Curiosity has been ascending since 2014.” This terrain could also indicate there was once water in Valle Grande, based on previous polygon patches: > Some of the polygons that the mission has spotted in the past clearly formed as mud cracks, though a variety of processes can contribute to their honeycomb textures, including cycles of warm and cold temperatures or compression that squeezed water out of the sediment when the surface was buried.

articles.title: Some Myotis bats can live 50 years while close relatives live just 7; sequencing eight species found longevity genes overlapping with cancer and virus defenses
articles.summary: Experiments & Discoveries News: A mouse-sized bat that lives for decades appears to have evolved some of the same biological protections that help it resist cancer and viral disease..
articles.body: A mouse-sized bat that lives for decades appears to have evolved some of the same biological protections that help it resist cancer and viral disease. Researchers comparing eight closely related Myotis species found an extraordinary range of lifespans, from about seven years in some species to nearly 50 years in others. Their genome analysis revealed that genes associated with longevity overlapped far more than expected with genes involved in virus interactions and cancer defence. As reported by ScienceDaily, the study suggests that long life in these bats may be connected to an immune system that can fight infection while also identifying and removing damaged cells. The findings do not offer an immediate treatment for human ageing, but they give scientists a new way to investigate how some mammals remain healthy for decades despite their small size and demanding lives.A small mammal with a long lifeIn mammals, body size often provides a rough clue to lifespan. Larger animals such as elephants and whales tend to live much longer than small mammals such as mice. Bats challenge that pattern.Some bats weigh only a few grams but can live for several decades. They fly, use large amounts of energy and face repeated exposure to viruses, yet certain species age slowly compared with similarly sized mammals. The little brown bat, Myotis lucifugus, is one of the longest lived members of the group studied by researchers.Close relatives in the same genus can have very different lifespans. Some Myotis species live only around seven years, while others can reach nearly 50. That contrast makes the genus an unusual natural experiment. The species share a common evolutionary history, but their lifespans have diverged substantially. The scientists hoped to be able to identify the genetic changes linked to longer life by comparing their genomes. They were not searching for one “longevity gene.” Instead, they looked for patterns across many genes and biological pathways.Sequencing eight Myotis speciesThe research team generated near-complete genome assemblies for eight closely related Myotis species. They also developed cell lines and conducted experiments using primary cells, allowing them to connect genetic patterns with cellular responses. The genome comparisons looked for signs of positive selection -- genetic changes that appear to have been favored by natural selection because they boosted survival or reproduction. The researchers also looked at structural variation, including differences in gene copy number between species. The findings suggested repeated adaptation in pathways related to longevity and cancer resistance. Long-lived lineages had stronger evolutionary signals in genes that help protect cells from damage and prevent malignant changes. The study also found that many genes associated with lifespan are involved in interactions with viruses. Some of these genes help viruses infect cells, while others help the host detect or control infection. Their overlap suggests that immune defence and longevity may have evolved together rather than as completely separate biological systems.The connection between viruses and ageingViruses place a constant burden on an animal’s immune system. A bat that lives for decades may encounter many viral infections during its lifetime. It needs to control those infections without creating excessive inflammation or damaging its own tissues. The researchers found that Myotis bats have an unusually large number of genes encoding proteins that interact with DNA viruses, including herpes viruses. Some of these proteins support viral replication, while others activate protective responses such as interferon production.The pattern was different for RNA viruses. Rather than showing the same genome-wide enrichment, Myotis bats displayed greater copy number variation in genes involved in RNA virus interactions. Copy number variation means that individuals or species may carry different numbers of copies of a gene. One important example is EIF2AK2, also known as PKR. This immune factor helps cells respond to viral genetic material and limit the production of proteins that viruses need. Researchers found that Myotis species can have one, two or three copies of PKR, suggesting that gene duplication may provide additional flexibility in antiviral defence.How cancer resistance enters the storyLong life creates a biological problem. The more years an animal lives, the more opportunities its cells have to accumulate mutations. A long-lived species would therefore be expected to face increased cancer risk unless it also evolves stronger mechanisms to control damaged cells.The Myotis genomes showed positive selection in cancer-related pathways. This suggests that as some species evolved longer lifespans, natural selection also strengthened systems for preventing or eliminating malignant cells.Cells from the long lived little brown bat provided further clues. When exposed to DNA damage, the cells showed a distinctive response involving the removal of severely damaged cells. Rather than allowing damaged cells to continue dividing, the system may encourage them to undergo programmed cell death.That approach can protect the organism from cancer by preventing a damaged cell from becoming a tumour. It may also reduce the risk that genetic damage accumulates across decades.The finding is important because it links longevity with quality control. Living longer is not only about slowing damage. It may also include spotting damage early and removing cells that can no longer be safely repaired. Why the overlap matters The researchers found more overlap than expected between genes associated with longevity and genes involved in viral interactions. That pattern suggests the same biological systems may have been shaped by multiple pressures. One gene that helps identify viral damage may also influence how cells respond to genetic damage from other sources. A mechanism that controls infection may affect inflammation, cell division or cancer risk. Evolution can therefore produce traits with several effects, a phenomenon known as pleiotropy.This does not mean every antiviral gene extends lifespan or that resistance to one virus automatically protects against cancer. The relationship is more complex. The study identifies patterns that point to shared mechanisms and offers hypotheses for future research. The connection is especially intriguing because bats need to maintain strong immune defences without suffering the chronic inflammation that can damage tissues. Their ability to tolerate viruses while limiting disease may be part of what allows some species to age slowly.What bat cells revealGenome data show which genes differ between species, but cell experiments help show what those differences may do. Researchers grew primary cells from Myotis bats and observed how the cells responded to damage and immune challenges.In the long-lived little brown bat, the response to DNA damage was unusual.Cells increased the activity of genes associated with cell death after serious damage rather than relying only on mechanisms that repair DNA. This may help remove cells that are too damaged to be safely restored.The finding does not prove that the same process explains the entire lifespan difference. Ageing involves metabolism, reproduction, inflammation, tissue maintenance and many other factors. However, it provides a biological mechanism that could contribute to cancer resistance in a long-lived species.Studying these mechanisms may also help scientists understand why some animals tolerate cellular stress better than others. Bats are not simply living longer because they avoid damage. They may be managing damage more effectively.Possible lessons for human healthResearchers hope that bat biology can eventually reveal new approaches to ageing-related disease, cancer and viral infections. If scientists identify the molecules that help bat cells respond to damage, those pathways might inspire medicines or therapies.That possibility remains distant. A bat gene cannot simply be transferred into a human treatment, and biological systems that work in bats may have different effects in people. Researchers would need to understand how the pathways operate, whether they can be safely modified and how they interact with human immune systems.The most immediate value lies in basic science. By studying species that are naturally cancer resistant and healthy for decades, scientists can discover mechanisms that may be difficult to find by studying standard lab animals alone. Bats also present an opportunity to study trade-offs. A strong immune response can be protective, but over-activation can lead to inflammation. Myotis species may have evolved a balance that controls infections while reducing damage to their own tissues.Not all Myotis bats age the same wayThe genus contains many species, and their lifespans differ considerably. That variation is essential to the study because it allows researchers to compare close relatives with different ageing patterns.A seven year lifespan and a nearly 50 year lifespan represent very different biological strategies. The shorter lived species may mature, reproduce and age more quickly, while the longer-lived species may invest more in cellular maintenance and immune regulation.Researchers can then use these contrasts to identify repeated patterns of evolution. When similar genetic changes are made in multiple long-lived lineages, these become stronger candidates for contributing to longevity. The study found repeated evolution of longevity associated with cancer pathways, suggesting that the relationship evolved more than once within Myotis. Repeated patterns are especially valuable because they are less likely to be accidental differences unrelated to lifespan.A window into healthy ageingThe Myotis study does not provide a simple formula for living to 100. It shows that longevity can emerge from a combination of traits that protect cells, control viruses and reduce cancer risk.The bats appear to have evolved immune systems that are unusually capable of dealing with infectious organisms while maintaining cellular stability. Their genomes also contain structural variations that may expand their ability to respond to different types of viruses. For humans, the wider lesson is that ageing is not controlled by one isolated process. Immunity, cancer defence, DNA damage, inflammation and cell death may be connected parts of a larger system.A small bat living for nearly 50 years challenges assumptions about what mammals of its size can achieve. Its genes are not a ready-made cure, but they offer clues to the biological strategies that make a long, healthy life possible.

articles.title: In 2016, a Montana researcher picked up a rock half the size of a golf ball; 10 years later, scans showed dinosaur dung holding the finest feather yet found from the age of dinosaurs
articles.summary: Archaeology & Ancient World News: Sometimes, the most extraordinary discoveries are hiding in things that look utterly ordinary. In 2016, a researcher working in Montana spotted a smal.
articles.body: Sometimes, the most extraordinary discoveries are hiding in things that look utterly ordinary. In 2016, a researcher working in Montana spotted a small, reddish-brown rock while searching for fossils. It was about half the size of a golf ball, hardly the kind of object that would seem destined for a major scientific discovery, states a study published by Science Daily. But a closer look revealed a tiny fossil feather on its surface. A decade later, advanced scans showed that the rock held a much bigger story: it was fossilized dinosaur dung containing remarkably preserved feathers, bones and scales, including what researchers describe as the finest feather specimen yet discovered from the age of dinosaurs. Scroll down to read the details.A 66-million-year-old findThe coprolite, or fossilized feces, dates to roughly 66 million years ago, near the end of the Cretaceous Period. Inside, researchers found several feathers along with tiny fish scales and leg bones belonging to a hesperornithiform, an extinct group of aquatic birds. The evidence suggests that a large dinosaur, potentially a T. rex or Nanotyrannus, had eaten the bird. The discovery offers an unusually intimate glimpse into an ancient food chain. Instead of reconstructing predator and prey relationships from separate fossils, scientists can see evidence of one animal's final meal preserved in a single specimen.The feather that survivedDavid DeMar Jr., a researcher with the University of Washington's Burke Museum, discovered the unusual nodule while conducting fieldwork in northeastern Montana's Hell Creek Formation. Researchers later suspected that the rock might be a coprolite, but its real significance became clear only after it was examined using micro-CT scanning. The technology allowed scientists to look inside the specimen without breaking it apart. The scans revealed a remarkable collection of remains — including feathers, bones and scales preserved in three dimensions. For lead author Jingmai O'Connor of Chicago's Field Museum, the discovery could help answer one of paleontology's biggest questions: why did some birds survive the asteroid impact that wiped out nearly all other dinosaurs?Why did some birds survive?When the asteroid struck Earth 66 million years ago, most dinosaur lineages disappeared. Among the birds, only the group known as Neornithes survived, eventually giving rise to every bird alive today. Scientists have proposed several explanations, including the possibility that aquatic habitats helped some birds withstand the environmental chaos that followed the impact. But the newly studied hesperornithiform complicates that theory. These birds were also closely associated with water, yet they went extinct. Instead, researchers believe their feathers may offer an important clue. The fossil shows a mixture of relatively modern-looking, waterproof feathers and smaller, primitive body feathers.Images Courtesy: istock

articles.title: Italy and wolves: living with a growing population amid myths and alarmism
articles.summary: The latest data put Italy's wolf population at around 3,500 animals spread nationwide, and experts say it has since grown. Amid sightings and scares, what is...
articles.body:
From the attacks in Puglia to sightings in Emilia-Romagna, Umbria and Lazio, the summer of 2026 was dominated by alarmism about wolves.

The wolves currently present in Italy are around 3,500 according to the data from the latest national monitoring exercise carried out by Ispra (source in Italian) , the Higher Institute for Environmental Protection and Research, which dates back to 2022. Since then the population has increased by around 150 animals, mainly in the Alpine area.

However, it is not only the growing number of wolves or the sightings near built-up areas that have reopened the debate about the species.

In March 2026 Italy transposed the 2025 EU directive on the wolf's protection status , which amends the previous 1992 rules. The animal has thus gone from "highly protected species" to "protected species", raising questions among experts about how useful this downgrading really is.

Are there too many wolves in Italy? How real is the risk for people living in towns and cities and how should they behave? Euronews asked experts in the field to respond, debunking myths and scaremongering.

"Wolf attacks remain an extremely rare phenomenon, so there is no real risk to people, but in recent years we have seen an increase in these cases, which we monitor very closely," says Piero Genovesi , head of the wildlife coordination service at Ispra, speaking to Euronews.

The institute was the first to carry out nationwide monitoring of the number and distribution of wolves in Italy using rigorous scientific methods. In the past, animals were counted at local and regional level on the basis of sightings and estimates, but the methods were not standardised.

Ispra's study was conducted between 2018 and 2022 and used a single protocol for sampling and data analysis across the country, as well as the most sophisticated statistical methods currently available. The figure of 3,500 animals is therefore an accurate estimate of the number of wolves actually present in the country; it is not a minimum figure, the experts stress.

"Numbers tell only part of the story: wolves are territorial animals that live in packs and they do not accept other animals in their territory. This means that numerical increases are not explosive, but that the species tends to colonise any area left free ," explains Genovesi, noting that the wolf has gone from being a species almost extinct 50 years ago to one that is now found virtually everywhere, from the beaches of Rome and Puglia to the Po Valley.

The species' remarkable adaptability is the reason why sightings near cities are no longer so rare.

There were 19 incidents of wolves attacking humans between 2017 and 2024, according to Ispra data gathered thanks to cooperation with Life Wild Wolf, (source in Italian) an EU co-financed project that supports the authorities in preventing and managing interactions between humans and wolves.

The most significant figure, however, concerns the number of wolves involved in these attacks: only seven animals were responsible for all the cases , and a single female wolf committed 11 of them. Looking at the numbers, it is clear that these episodes are exceptional and that these particular wolves have developed abnormal behaviour , as confirmed by experts and by studies that have been focusing on this species for decades.

"In reality there is no need to be afraid of wolves: it is a species that keeps its distance; it is a shy, nocturnal animal that tends to avoid coming into contact with humans ," says Marco Antonelli, zoologist and large carnivore specialist for WWF Italy.

Ispra has drawn up a specific protocol for the management of urban and 'confident' wolves , classifying wolf behaviour according to the level of risk it poses. While sightings near homes have always occurred and pose no risk, permanent settlements close to people carry a higher level of risk, up to increasingly worrying behaviour such as the predation of domestic animals and, ultimately, aggressive reactions towards humans.

"There may be different reasons why this kind of behaviour develops: certain human actions lead wolves to become used to and comfortable around people ," explains Antonelli, adding that in some cases these are individual traits of specific animals that develop behaviour that departs from the norm.

Downlisting and legislation in other European countries

The major novelty in 2026 is the so-called "downlisting", the move from the category of "highly protected" species to "protected" species . The difference is just a single word, but we will have to wait and see what changes in practice.

In March Italy approved the transposition of the 2025 EU directive and will have to bring previous rules into line with it by January 2027 . The decision is triggering a wave of changes at national level: Germany, for example, has already transposed the new directive and is preparing to amend its national hunting law.

"It was a political choice, pushed by President von der Leyen . It was not necessary; wolves could already be culled under derogation, as provided for in the legislation," says Luigi Boitani , emeritus professor at La Sapienza University in Rome and one of the world's leading wolf experts.

His view is backed up by some figures: in Italy there have been cases of culls authorised as derogations from the rules, and there are countries where they took place regularly, such as France, which culled 250 wolves every year .

According to Piero Genovesi, by contrast, in the Italian system the downgrading brings technical changes, as it simplifies the bureaucratic procedure .

"Whereas previously authorisation from the Environment Ministry was required, based on a technical opinion from Ispra, now the regions can decide autonomously, still on the basis of a technical opinion," says Genovesi.

The current system should therefore be much more flexible, but it does not solve the real problem created by the growing number of wolves in Europe.

"The downgrading was essentially a political decision driven by very powerful farming lobbies at European level, in an attempt to solve the age-old issue of conflict between wolves and livestock farming ," says Marco Antonelli, speaking to Euronews.

The difficult coexistence between wolves and farmers

Zootechnics is the science that deals with livestock breeding. And it is livestock farmers who have always been on the front line in denouncing the damage caused by wolves to their sector and the dangers faced by farm animals.

"Over the past 10 years, wolves are thought to have been responsible for preying on 0.6% of the livestock present in Europe , and the figures for Italy are very similar," says Antonelli, adding that the phenomenon should not be underestimated and should in fact be tackled with appropriate prevention strategies.

One of the most effective strategies is the use of so-called livestock guardian dogs , specially selected breeds of sheepdogs that look after and guard flocks. One of the best breeds for this job is found in Italy: the Maremma-Abruzzese sheepdog.

Other, more modern strategies include electrified and buried fences or raised night shelters , which provide effective protection for animals. Culls can be a solution to deal with animals that develop abnormal behaviour, but taken together these protective measures can ensure everyday coexistence between wolves and farmers.

"The data show that prevention strategies are much more effective than any culling strategy . A solution does exist, but it is not as simple as many make out, which is why the commitment of the authorities is also needed," Antonelli concludes.

Beyond polarisation: "coexistence means compromise"

City dwellers can also play a part and need to know the right preventive behaviour to adopt. Above all, it is essential to ensure proper waste disposal, as rubbish is highly attractive to all kinds of wildlife.

Another important factor is the management of pets: in areas where sightings are frequent, experts advise against leaving pets unattended and, above all, against leaving pet food on the street, as it could attract wolves.

"The most dramatic change we are seeing today is the polarisation of opinion about wolves : the number of people wanting to defend them has grown a lot, and so has the number of people wanting to see them culled," says Luigi Boitani.

"The middle ground is still very small, yet that is what we should be aiming for: coexistence means compromise ," the professor concludes. Knowledge of the species beyond opinions and myths is still limited, but pursuing it is the only long-term solution.

articles.title: Britain’s wasps are unusually scarce this summer; researchers cannot find enough for experiments, and the few seen are unusually small
articles.summary: Wildlife & Biodiversity News: Britain’s summer is missing one of its most familiar insects. Wasps that usually gather around outdoor food, patrol gardens and become increasingly no.
articles.body: Britain’s summer is missing one of its most familiar insects. Wasps that usually gather around outdoor food, patrol gardens and become increasingly noticeable in late summer appear unusually scarce in 2026. The shortage has become so pronounced that researchers are struggling to collect enough insects for laboratory experiments, while the few wasps being seen appear smaller than expected for the season. Scientists suspect that a combination of volatile spring weather, repeated heatwaves and reduced food supplies may have disrupted colonies before they could grow. As reported by ScienceDaily, the evidence is not yet based on the country’s main national survey, so researchers are treating the pattern cautiously. Even so, the unusual absence is drawing attention because wasps are important predators, pollinators and decomposers, not simply unwanted picnic visitors.A summer without the usual buzzFor many people, the absence of wasps may sound like good news. Fewer insects around outdoor meals means fewer stings, fewer nest removal requests and less anxiety during warm weather. Yet wasps play important roles in ecosystems, and their disappearance may signal changes that are more significant than a quieter garden. Social wasps eat caterpillars, flies and other insects, helping to control populations that can harm plants and crops. The adults also forage flowers for nectar, aiding in pollination. When wasps die, their bodies and remains of their prey become part of nutrient cycles, making them decomposers as well as predators. Their seasonal abundance tends to follow a familiar pattern. Queens emerge in spring, found nests and produce workers. The colony grows through summer, eventually producing reproductive males and queens. By late summer, workers are often highly visible as natural food sources decline and they search for sugar near homes, gardens and outdoor gatherings.This year, that pattern appears disrupted. The insects are not simply arriving late in some places. Researchers and pest control professionals are reporting noticeably lower activity.Scientists struggle to find specimensThe shortage has been particularly obvious to wasp biologists. Researchers need live wasps for experiments examining behaviour, ecology, communication and colony organisation. This year, students have struggled to find enough insects for planned studies.That difficulty offers an unusual form of evidence. Scientists who work with wasps know where and when to look for them, and they are familiar with normal seasonal activity. When experienced researchers cannot collect specimens, the absence becomes difficult to dismiss as a casual impression. However, anecdotal evidence is not the same as a national population estimate. The Big Wasp Survey, the United Kingdom’s main public monitoring project for wasps, had not yet begun collecting its 2026 summer samples when the reports emerged. Until those data are available, researchers cannot say precisely how much populations have declined or whether the pattern affects the entire country equally.Some areas may have normal numbers while others experience severe shortages. Local weather, habitat and food availability can all influence colony success. Scientists therefore need systematic sampling before drawing firm conclusions.A strange springThe possible explanation begins with the weather earlier in the year. Spring 2026 started with warm, dry conditions that would normally favour wasp colonies. Warm weather can help queens forage, develop eggs and find prey for their larvae. Dry periods may also reduce the risk of nests being damaged by persistent rain.But the season then became unusually unstable. Periods of extreme heat were interrupted by sudden cold and damp weather and surprisingly cool nights. Such rapid changes can be hard on insects whose activity and development is triggered by temperature. A queen establishing a nest during a warm spell could find herself in trouble if cold or wet weather hits unexpectedly. She may abandon the nest, die while foraging or fail to raise enough workers to support colony growth. If many queens are affected at the beginning of the season, the consequences can continue for months.Instead of a strong spring population expanding into large summer colonies, the country may have started the season with fewer successful nests. Repeated heatwaves could then have added further pressure.The heat limit of waspsEvery insect has a critical thermal maximum, often called CTmax. This is the approximate temperature beyond which the animal begins to lose normal function and may suffer dehydration, muscle spasms, immobility or death.Researchers estimate that social wasps may have a CTmax of around 45 degrees Celsius. That is lower than the tolerance reported for some other social insects, including honeybees. Air temperatures do not tell the whole story because ground surfaces, pavement, roofs and exposed soil can become much hotter than the air.A wasp colony may therefore experience dangerous conditions even when the official air temperature appears only moderately extreme. Nests exposed to direct sunlight can overheat, while foraging workers may struggle to find shade or water.Heat can affect different stages of the colony. Adults may become stressed or dehydrated, while larvae depend on workers to bring food and regulate nest conditions. A prolonged hot period can disrupt both the individual insects and the social system that keeps the colony functioning.Why the remaining wasps look smallResearchers have also noticed that the wasps being seen appear unusually small. In a normal late summer, many workers should be larger than the early season individuals that emerge from newly established nests. Instead, some of the insects still look “spring sized.”Several explanations are possible. Larvae may be receiving less food if prey populations are limited. Adult workers need protein rich insects to feed developing larvae, and a shortage could restrict growth. Dry conditions may also reduce the number of caterpillars, flies and other prey available around nests.Temperature itself may play a role. The 2026 observations are particularly interesting because of that possibility. Insects reared at the higher temperatures might develop faster and reach the pupal stage at a smaller size. Faster development might allow larvae to complete their life cycle before conditions become lethal, but the adults that emerge might be smaller. Researchers may be seeing not only fewer wasps but also a physical change associated with heat stress. If similar patterns appear in future years, smaller body size could become one way to observe the effects of climate change on social insects.A warning for ecosystemsThe decline is not yet confirmed as a nationwide collapse, but it raises concerns about ecological consequences. Wasps are important natural enemies of other insects. Without predatory wasps, gardeners and farmers could see more caterpillars or flies, but pest populations are influenced by many factors. Wasps have relationships with plants and other animals, too. Adults consume nectar, but their nests also host complex social communities. The removal of one group from a food web can have consequences for species that feed upon them or compete with them for resources. The importance may extend beyond wasps. If extreme heat and volatile weather are impacting colonies, other insects with similar thermal limits or food requirements may also be under duress. Insects are central to pollination, decomposition and nutrient cycling, so changes in their abundance can influence whole ecosystems.A single unusual summer does not establish a long term trend. But repeated extremes can gradually reshape populations, especially when insects face habitat loss, pesticides, disease and reduced food supplies at the same time.Measuring what is happeningThe Big Wasp Survey will be important for determining whether the reports match national patterns. Public participants collect wasps using standardised methods, allowing scientists to compare abundance and species across regions and years. Such surveys can reveal whether the shortage affects common social wasps, solitary species or both. They can also show whether some parts of Britain have higher numbers because of local habitat, rainfall or temperatures.Researchers will need more than counts. Measuring body size, colony development and reproductive success can help identify the mechanisms behind the change. If wasps are smaller, scientists can examine whether the difference is linked to prey availability, larval temperature or other environmental conditions. Long term monitoring is especially important as climate patterns become less predictable. A short survey can capture a snapshot, but repeated observations reveal whether an unusual year is an isolated event or part of a broader decline.A complicated relationship with waspsPeople often view wasps mainly as pests, especially when workers become persistent around food and drinks in late summer. Their stings can be painful and dangerous for people with allergies. Managing nests near homes and public spaces remains important. That understandable concern can obscure their ecological value. The same insects that disturb picnics also hunt pests, pollinate flowers and contribute to decomposition. A healthy environment does not require people to welcome wasps inside their homes, but it does depend on recognising that they are part of a larger system. The strange summer of 2026 is a chance to reconsider that relationship. A less boisterous season may be convenient, but it should also prompt questions about what is different. If weather extremes are disrupting wasp colonies, the absence could be an early sign of stress that affects other species later.What comes nextScientists will continue looking for wasps, measuring their size and waiting for the national survey data. The results may confirm that populations are unusually low, reveal strong regional differences or show that the apparent decline was concentrated in particular habitats.Until then, researchers are avoiding definitive claims. The evidence is striking, but it remains preliminary. Weather, prey availability, disease and local habitat conditions may all have contributed to the pattern.The few small wasps seen this summer may therefore represent more than an odd seasonal curiosity. They could provide a glimpse of how insects respond when heatwaves, cold snaps and food shortages arrive in quick succession. Britain’s wasp population may recover in a cooler or more stable year, but the 2026 observations show how vulnerable even familiar insects can be when climate conditions move beyond their usual range.

articles.title: EPA to repeal limits on greenhouse gas emissions from power plants
articles.summary: The move would overturn a 2024 Biden administration rule requiring power plants to control planet-warming pollution.
articles.body: The Environmental Protection Agency announced Monday that it will roll back emissions limits on coal- and gas-fired power plants — one of the Trump administration’s most significant moves yet to undo the climate policies enacted under Presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama. The change would overturn a 2024 rule requiring power plants to use carbon sequestration equipment to control pollution; it was one of the biggest climate change rules implemented by the Biden administration’s EPA. The agency also proposed eliminating all other greenhouse gas emissions rules, arguing that under the Clean Air Act, it doesn’t have the authority to regulate those emissions as they pertain to climate change. In February, the EPA similarly repealed emissions rules for vehicles, which account for the most pollution in the U.S. today. The agency repealed greenhouse gas emissions standards for vehicles, as well as the legal conclusion that underpins its obligation to regulate such emissions in the first place, known as the endangerment finding. The moves announced Monday would essentially do the same thing for power plants, which are the second-biggest source of U.S. emissions. If the newly announced rollbacks survive the expected legal challenges, they could prevent future administrations from requiring coal and gas power plants to limit planet-warming pollution. “It’s part of a thematic effort to roll back air quality standards,” said Charles Driscoll, a professor of environmental systems and engineering at Syracuse University. “Trump has said he doesn’t believe in climate change, so he’s been working hard to try to roll back any sort of carbon control measures that have been implemented previously or might be implemented in the future.” The announcement came during a meeting of energy ministers about “energy abundance” at the G20 summit in Houston. The EPA said repealing the 2024 power-plant rule would save industry more than $300 billion in costs and help “unleash” American energy. “The Trump administration has come in to protect American energy and to make sure you can afford to keep the lights on,” EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said in a statement. Industry groups cheered the announcement. “Overturning these examples of EPA overreach will help preserve and strengthen the U.S. coal fleet, protect grid reliability, and shield electricity consumers from higher costs at a time of surging demand from data centers, artificial intelligence, and advanced manufacturing,” Michelle Bloodworth, a spokesperson for America’s Power, a trade organization for the country’s fleet of more than 400 coal-fired power plants, said in a statement. Environmental groups have already sued the Trump administration to challenge its repeal of the endangerment finding. They promised to sue in response to the changes announced Monday, as well. “This is full-throated climate denial,” said Patrick Drupp, the climate policy director at the Sierra Club. “It’s going to mean more pollution, more extreme weather, higher electricity bills because we’re going to continue to rely on fossil fuels. ... This is the administration doubling and tripling down on old fossil-fueled coal and gas.” The Biden administration’s 2024 rule was designed to be phased in over time. It would have required power plants to sequester and store at least 90% of the carbon pollution they produced by 2032. The administration said at the time that the requirement would benefit the climate and public health in ways that would far outweigh the implementation costs. The administration estimated that in the year 2035 alone, the rule would be responsible for preventing 1,200 premature deaths, 360,000 cases of asthma symptoms and 47,000 lost workdays. The Trump administration is reversing the policy when the consequences of climate change — intense heat waves and stronger storms, for example — are becoming more obvious. Extreme heat has baked much of the world this summer. July was the hottest month on record in the U.S., according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and many locations set all-time records. Overall, the three months from June through August were the warmest ever recorded for the contiguous United States. Last year was the third-hottest in modern history, according to Copernicus, the European Union’s climate monitoring service. The past 11 years have been the 11 warmest on record, Copernicus data shows. The litigation over the new EPA policy changes could take years and might not resolve before President Donald Trump leaves office. “These cases proceed relatively slowly in the courts of appeals,” said Meghan Greenfield, a partner at the law firm Jenner & Block who oversaw the EPA’s Supreme Court docket for rulemaking during the Biden administration. “It’s not clear to me at this point that this repeal, the one that’s being finalized today, will be before the Supreme Court by the end of this administration.”

articles.title: Study finds drylands could spread across 40% of Earth's land by 2100, with Australia hit hardest
articles.summary: Parts of Africa are also expected to undergo notable shifts.
articles.body:
Research suggests that 40% of the world's land could become drylands by the end of the 21st century, impacting ecosystems.

Global drylands are projected to expand from about 38.58% to between 39.31% and 40.28% by 2071 to 2100, with carbon dioxide potentially affecting the spread.

Human activity is driving rising temperatures, leading to water scarcity, ecosystem degradation, and desertification in dryland regions, necessitating sustainable development and climate adaptation efforts.

Research has indicated that 40% of the world's land could shift into drylands by the end of the 21st century.

A study published in the journal Environmental Research Letters projected that global drylands could expand from about 38.58% of Earth's land area outside Antarctica during the 1994 to 2023 baseline period to between 39.31% and 40.28% by 2071 to 2100, according to ScienceAlert . It's a change that would alter ecosystems.

Using meteorological records from 1960 to 2023 alongside CMIP6 climate models, the researchers estimated how dryland areas may change over time. They treated places with an aridity index below 0.65 as drylands — a classification based on having relatively little rainfall compared with water losses from evaporation and plant activity.

In some scenarios, the researchers found that carbon dioxide — the main driver of rising global temperatures — could slightly curb the projected spread of drylands. As CO2 concentrations rise, plants often partly close tiny pores known as stomata, which reduces water loss through transpiration.

"Conventional projections often neglect CO2 effects on potential evapotranspiration, which may yield higher aridity estimates and alter aridity-change hotspot patterns," the authors wrote.

The study found that hyper-arid zones are expected to see the largest increase, while the upper end of the projections would amount to about 915,000 square miles (2.37 million square kilometers) compared with the 1994 to 2023 baseline.

As drylands expand, water scarcity can worsen, ecosystems can degrade, and communities and agriculture may find it harder to adapt to a hotter world. Regions already living close to the edge of water stress may have even less room for error as conditions continue to change.

ScienceAlert reported that the researchers predicted Australia will experience the most severe dryland changes, with Brazil next. Parts of Africa are also expected to undergo notable shifts. The paper said China and Russia contain extensive dry sub-humid zones, while Algeria, Libya, and Saudi Arabia are home to hyper-arid areas.

"Expansion of dryland climatic conditions into formerly more humid regions may aggravate water scarcity, ecosystem degradation and desertification, posing challenges to global sustainable development," the researchers wrote.

Human activity remains the underlying driver of rising temperatures, which increase evaporative demand and can push already water-stressed regions toward greater aridity. The most powerful long-term mitigation is rapidly reducing planet-warming pollution.

Restoration and conservation efforts through native vegetation, reforestation, improving soil organic matter, controlling erosion, and rebuilding watersheds are crucial. Healthy soil can hold more water, support more vegetation, and be more resilient during drought.

"Given the high ecological vulnerability of drylands, updated assessments of dryland extent and future redistribution are needed to support climate adaptation and sustainable development," the team added.

The projections line up with changes already playing out on the ground, from cropland degradation in dry regions to drought-driven displacement. They also tie into efforts to rebuild soils and manage carbon so landscapes can better hold up as aridity spreads.

• Across vulnerable farming regions, soil degradation is already here , shrinking arable land as climates dry.

• Catastrophic drought leaves land barren and pushes more Syrian families toward displacement.

• Farmers are treating soil as a climate solution , storing carbon while protecting moisture and nutrients.

Expanding dry conditions are reshaping land, livelihoods, and adaptation strategies. Without appropriate intervention, drylands will keep spreading.

articles.title: Buscar agua potable en el desierto ya no es imposible: un equipo de científicos ha logrado construir una máquina que genera 35 litros al día sin necesidad de baterías
articles.standfirst: Este grupo de expertos pertenece a la Universidad de California en Berkeley
articles.summary: Este grupo de expertos pertenece a la Universidad de California en Berkeley
articles.body: Cuando queremos dejar claro que algo es imposible, utilizamos el refrán ‘encontrar una gota de agua en el desierto’. Pues bien, científicos de la Universidad de California en Berkeley han convertido que este hecho pase a ser posible. Lo han logrado construyendo una máquina que extrajo vapor de agua del aire y acabó recolectando 35 litros al día de agua potable. No lo hicieron en pruebas sin valor en el interior de un laboratorio, sino que se trasladaron hasta el Parque Nacional del Valle de la Muerte, en Norteamérica. O lo que es lo mismo, uno de los lugares del planeta más calurosos. La máquina ‘convirtió’ el vapor de agua en agua potable. Además, lo hizo sin baterías ni enchufes, sólo con la energía del sol. Para construir este aparato, han hecho uso de un MOF (Metal-Organic Framework o estructura metalorgánica). Es un material cristalino formado por iones o grupos metálicos unidos mediante moléculas orgánicas. La característica principal de un elemento como este es que tiene una estructura muy porosa, capaz de atrapar y almacenar en diferentes moléculas. Es por eso que, principalmente, un MOF tiene aplicaciones como la captura y almacenamiento de gases, la separación de sustancias, la filtración y la detección de moléculas. El empleado en este dispositivo es una evolución, conocido como MOF-103, más preparado para absorber las moléculas de agua presentes en el aire. Así pues, hay que tener en cuenta que durante la noche, cuando aumenta la humedad del desierto, el material recoge el agua. Por el contrario, durante el día, el calor provocado por la luz solar hace que el agua se libere en forma de vapor. Este vapor se enfría, se condensa y finalmente se recoge en un recipiente. Un proceso que ha proporcionado 35 litros de agua potable al día.

articles.title: In 2013, California began removing millions of purple urchins from barren reefs; seven years later, more than 55 acres of kelp forest had returned
articles.summary: Nature & Environment News: Beneath the waves off Southern California, a once-lush underwater forest had been reduced to something resembling a desert. Kelp that had provided she.
articles.body: Beneath the waves off Southern California, a once-lush underwater forest had been reduced to something resembling a desert. Kelp that had provided shelter and food for fish, crabs and marine mammals had disappeared, leaving behind rocky reefs covered by hungry purple sea urchins. Then, in 2013, conservationists and fishermen began tackling the problem from the seafloor, one urchin at a time. Seven years later, more than 55 acres of kelp forest had returned, bringing marine life back with it, reports NOAA Fisheries website. Scroll down to read the details.When Kelp forests disappearKelp forests are among the most productive ecosystems in the ocean. They provide habitat for fish and invertebrates while supporting marine mammals and other wildlife.But Southern California's kelp forests have faced years of pressure from environmental damage. One major source of contamination came from the Montrose Chemical manufacturing plant, which discharged pollutants including DDT and PCBs into coastal waters between the 1940s and 1970s. The chemicals persisted in sediments along the Palos Verdes ocean shelf and affected marine ecosystems and wildlife. As kelp declined, another problem took hold.Purple Urchins take overAccording to the report, sea urchins normally form part of a healthy coastal ecosystem. But when their numbers become excessive, they can consume kelp faster than the plants can recover. The result is an urchin barren, a shallow reef where dense populations of purple urchins graze away newly growing kelp, preventing the forest from returning. To break that cycle, the Bay Foundation led a partnership involving researchers, conservationists and commercial urchin fishermen. Beginning in 2013, the team started removing the overwhelming numbers of purple urchins from affected reefs. The scale of the effort was enormous. Five commercial fishermen eventually contributed more than 8,000 hours of underwater work and harvested approximately 4.2 million urchins.Turning a barren reef green againThe goal was not simply to remove urchins. It was to give kelp a chance to establish itself and rebuild the habitat. The strategy began producing visible results. By 2020, restoration efforts had helped bring back more than 55 acres of kelp forest. The recovering forests created new habitat for fish and other marine species, transforming areas that had once been dominated by bare rock and urchins into more complex and productive ecosystems. The project also demonstrated the value of bringing people with different kinds of expertise to the same conservation problem. Scientists contributed research and monitoring, conservation groups coordinated restoration, and commercial fishermen brought years of practical experience working underwater.Restoration beyond KelpThe Kelp recovery is part of a much broader effort to repair ecosystems damaged by pollution and oil spills. In San Francisco Bay, restoration funds following the 2007 Cosco Busan oil spill have supported more than 60 projects. The spill contaminated more than 3,300 acres of shoreline habitat and affected Pacific herring. Among the projects have been efforts to restore subtidal eelgrass and native oyster habitat. More than nine acres of eelgrass have been planted, while more than five acres of oyster reef structures have been installed to provide habitat for oysters, fish, crabs, birds and other wildlife.A bigger lesson from damaged watersOther restoration work has extended south into Baja California, where conservation teams have worked to rebuild seabird populations affected by pollution and oil spills. On Pacific islands in the region, a multi-year restoration program used techniques designed to encourage seabirds to return while reducing human disturbance. Of 27 seabird populations that had disappeared from the islands, 22 have returned over the past decade, with four additional species beginning to nest there. These projects show that environmental recovery rarely happens through a single intervention. It can require years of monitoring, funding, fieldwork and cooperation between scientists, governments, conservation groups and local communities.Image Courtesy: Enric Sala, National Geographic

articles.title: Michigan scientists covered invasive zebra mussels with weighted lakebed mats and pumped carbon dioxide underneath; after five days, mortality of caged mussels topped 80%
articles.summary: Experiments & Discoveries News: Zebra mussels are small, but their impact on freshwater ecosystems can be enormous. Once established, the invasive shellfish can blanket lakebeds, cro.
articles.body: Zebra mussels are small, but their impact on freshwater ecosystems can be enormous. Once established, the invasive shellfish can blanket lakebeds, crowd out native species and alter the communities that depend on them. Scientists in Michigan are now testing a surprisingly simple idea: cover the lakebed and turn up the carbon dioxide underneath. A 2024 experiment at Loon Lake in Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore tested whether carbon dioxide could make benthic mats—a kind of heavy, flexible cover placed over the lake bottom—more effective at killing zebra mussels. The results suggest that the combination can work considerably faster than mats alone.Testing the mats in Loon LakeResearchers from the U.S. Geological Survey divided three areas of Loon Lake into treatment and reference plots. Each treatment area measured 4 by 4 meters, while the mats themselves were slightly larger to ensure that the lakebed was covered. The scientists tested two approaches. One used a polyethylene mat the experimental plots before treatment began. They then with a vinyl coating, anchored to the bottom with sandbags and weights. The second used an identical mat, but with carbon dioxide-infused water pumped underneath it.To measure the effects, researchers placed roughly 360 zebra mussels in cages across the experimental plots before treatment began. They then left the mats in place for five days before removing them and assessing mussel survival and the surrounding aquatic community.Carbon dioxide and pH measurementsThe ordinary mat did have an effect, but adding carbon dioxide produced a much stronger result. Under the carbon dioxide mats, concentrations reached levels close to 200 milligrams per liter, with pH measurements indicating sustained exposure during the treatment period. After five days, more than 80 percent of the caged zebra mussels in the carbon dioxide plots had died. By comparison, average mortality was 20.6 percent beneath the ordinary benthic mats and 12.7 percent in untreated reference plots.Researchers also found very few zebra mussels in the carbon dioxide and ordinary mat plots after treatment, with the lowest survival occurring where carbon dioxide had been introduced.Why carbon dioxide?The approach is based partly on earlier laboratory research suggesting that carbon dioxide can be more harmful to zebra mussels than to some native freshwater mussels. That selectivity matters. Eliminating an invasive species is of limited value if the treatment causes comparable damage to native wildlife. Previous experiments found that certain native unionid mussels could survive carbon dioxide exposures that were lethal to zebra mussels, although prolonged exposure could affect growth and tissue condition.The Michigan study therefore explored carbon dioxide as a potential selective toxin, using the mat to keep the treatment concentrated near the lakebed rather than dispersing it throughout the surrounding water.Native life still needs watchingThe results were encouraging, but the treatment was not without ecological effects. Researchers recorded lower total numbers of benthic macroinvertebrates—the small, tying up equipment and treatment areas for longer periods. If carbon dioxide can achieve high zebra mussel mortality in just a few days, the same equipment could potentially be moved animals living on or near the lakebed—in both types of mat plots compared with reference areas. Interestingly, however, overall diversity remained comparable among the treatments.That finding points to an important question for future work: whether carbon dioxide treatment can be refined enough to kill zebra mussels while minimizing disruption to other organisms living in the same habitat.A potentially faster control methodOne advantage of the carbon dioxide approach is speed. Conventional benthic mats can require extended deployment, tying up equipment and treatment areas for longer periods. If carbon dioxide can achieve high zebra mussel mortality in just a few days, the same equipment could potentially be moved and redeployed multiple times.The researchers say improvements to the carbon dioxide delivery system could also expand the area that can be treated at once.For now, the Loon Lake experiment is an early step rather than a universal solution. But it offers an intriguing new tool for managing zebra mussels: instead of relying solely on a physical barrier, scientists can transform the space beneath the mat into a short-lived, hostile environment for one of freshwater's most persistent invaders.Image Courtesy: istock

articles.title: Sento Segarra, experto en suplementos, aplaude la creatina y aconseja cuál comprar: "Es una carga rápida, es puro valor"

articles.summary: El divulgador afirma que es uno de los suplementos más contrastados y beneficiosos
articles.body: Sento Segarra, divulgador científico y experto en suplementos, ha alabado los efectos de la creatina. Tanto para las personas habituadas a hacer deporte, desde aficionados a profesionales, como para las que buscan reactivar su rendimiento cognitivo. En una entrevista en el pódcast 'Tengo un plan', el especialista ha negado tajantemente que las alabanzas a la creatina sean humo: "Es puro valor". Sento Segarra ha explicado el impacto a nivel visual de la creatina y ha argumentado por qué algunas personas se ven más fuertes en el espejo al tomarla. "No te estás dopando. La creatina, en las personas que van al gimnasio, hace que retengan un poquito más de agua dentro del músculo y coge cuerpo. Por eso te ves más fuerte", ha reflexionado ante las preguntas de los entrevistadores. La creatina puede hacer que ganes algo de peso en la báscula, pero en ningún caso es destacable: "Puedes pesar un poquito más, pero es poco. Lo que debes tener es mucha hidratación porque ese agua está saliendo de algún sitio, del torrente sanguíneo y depositándose en el músculo para que tengas ese aspecto cachas". El origen de la creatina, según ha recordado Sento Segarra, se remonta a la década de los 90, en los gimnasios: "Sólo se hacían experimentos en hombres porque era para ponerse cachas. Sí que es verdad que la creatina mejora el rendimiento. Nuestros músculos gastan energía y la energía en el cuerpo es una molécula que se llama ATP. Cuando pierde un fosfato, simplificado al máximo, libera energía". "Cuando pierde el fosfato se llama ADP, es como una pila descargada, ya no sirve para nada. Lo que tiene que pasar es que debe volver a recargarse", ha añadido. Las formas de conseguir de nuevo esta energía, ha detallado el experto en suplementos, son dos: "Con consumo de glucosa o bien de repente está la señora creatina que tiene un fosfato y se lo pasa otra vez a la ATP. Digamos que es una carga rápida". Sento Segarra ha apuntado que la creatina también tiene beneficios a nivel cognitivo: "Eso, que se sabe que pasa en los músculos, se sabe también que pasa en la cabeza. Mejora muchísimo. En la gente joven no funciona tan bien como en la gente mayor. La gente joven tiene los depósitos de creatina más llenos. Si tienes algo lleno, aunque le eches no vas a conseguir esa mejora. Pero en una persona mayor, que tiene el depósito a la mitad... Estás consiguiendo un despertar, una energía rápida, esa chispa". Sento Segarra, experto en suplementación, ha dado las claves para decidir qué creatina comprar: "La creatina tiene que ser monohidratada. Si lleva el sello creapure, pues mejor. ¿Es necesario el sello creapure? Si la marca es de garantía, pues a lo mejor la diferencia de precio no te vale tanto la pena. Si eres deportista de élite, creapure porque vas a evitar sustos. Me da una garantía del 99 por ciento de pureza y un montón de historias, pero es que la diferencia de precio es abismal".

articles.title: Arizona’s Apache trout was pushed toward extinction by habitat loss and non-native trout; after decades of recovery it was delisted, and a new barrier protects 22 miles of habitat
articles.summary: Wildlife & Biodiversity News: Arizona’s Apache trout has made a remarkable recovery after decades of pressure from habitat degradation, overfishing and introduced trout. The native.
articles.body: Arizona’s Apache trout has made a remarkable recovery after decades of pressure from habitat degradation, overfishing and introduced trout. The native fish was once close to disappearing from the cold mountain streams of eastern Arizona, but long-term conservation led by the White Mountain Apache Tribe and supported by state and federal partners helped rebuild its populations. According to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS), the Apache trout was officially removed from the federal list of threatened and endangered species in September 2024 after meeting recovery goals. The latest milestone is the completion of a new barrier on Big Bonito Creek, which now protects nearly 22 miles of stream habitat from invading non-native trout.A native trout facing multiple threatsThe Apache trout is found naturally only in the mountain streams of eastern Arizona, particularly around the White Mountains. It is one of only two trout species native to Arizona and is also the state fish. The species depends on cold, clean streams flowing through mountain forests and meadows. Its decline began long before modern conservation programmes were established.The fish faced pressure from overfishing, habitat degradation caused by activities such as timber harvesting, road construction and grazing, as well as wildfires. However, one of the most serious threats came from trout that had been introduced into Arizona waters for fishing and other purposes. Introduced brook and brown trout could compete with Apache trout for food and habitat, and they could prey on them. Rainbow and cutthroat trout created another problem because they could hybridise with Apache trout, threatening the genetic identity of the native fish. The combination of these pressures pushed the species towards extinction and eventually led to federal protection.Conservation began before federal protectionOne of the most important parts of the Apache trout recovery story began in 1955, before the Endangered Species Act existed. The White Mountain Apache Tribe recognised that native trout populations were declining and closed fishing in reservation waters containing remaining Apache trout populations. That early intervention helped protect some of the last surviving populations. Conservation work later expanded to include habitat restoration, captive propagation, removal of non-native fish and construction of barriers designed to keep invasive trout away from Apache trout streams.The Apache trout was listed as endangered in 1967 under the federal Endangered Species Preservation Act and later received protection under the Endangered Species Act in 1973. In 1975, it was downlisted from endangered to threatened after conservation efforts helped establish additional populations. Over the following decades, the recovery programme expanded across tribal, state and federal lands.Reaching the goal for recoveryThe recovery effort eventually reached a major benchmark. According to USFWS, the recovery plan called for 30 genetically pure, self-sustaining populations with sufficient habitat. A species status assessment completed in 2022 confirmed that this goal had been achieved. The progress was the result of decades of cooperation involving the White Mountain Apache Tribe, Arizona Game and Fish Department, USFWS, U.S. Forest Service, Trout Unlimited and other partners.In September 2024, the Apache trout was officially removed from the federal list because of its recovery. USFWS describes it as the first sport fish and first trout species to be delisted from federal protections because its populations had recovered. But delisting did not mean the conservation work was finished.New barrier protects 22 miles of habitatA key part of continuing that protection is preventing non-native trout from moving back into streams where Apache trout have recovered. The Big Bonito Creek Barrier was originally built decades ago to prevent non-native trout from moving upstream into Apache trout habitat. Over time, the old structure deteriorated and could no longer provide the protection required.USFWS and its partners therefore helped fund its replacement. The new barrier was completed in 2025 and is designed to protect nearly 22 miles of stream habitat. According to the agency, that represents roughly 18% of all remaining Apache trout recovery habitat. The project involved funding and support from the White Mountain Apache Tribe, the Arizona Fish and Wildlife Conservation Office, the Desert Fish Habitat Partnership, the Bureau of Reclamation, the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation and other USFWS programmes.Keeping invasive trout outBarriers are only one part of the strategy. Conservation teams also actively remove non-native trout from Apache trout waters. Biologists use backpack-mounted electrofishing equipment to capture and remove invasive fish. Environmental DNA, or eDNA, sampling can then be used to identify traces of non-native trout that may remain in streams. This allows crews to target areas where additional removal is needed.Other fish-passage projects are also being developed to improve connectivity within Apache trout habitat. One USFWS project involves removing or replacing outdated barriers and culverts, with the potential to reopen more than 52 miles of habitat while creating larger connected populations. The challenge is therefore a careful balancing act: some barriers are essential because they keep invasive trout out, while others can be removed when they unnecessarily fragment native fish habitat.A recovery that still requires protectionThe Apache trout’s return from the edge of extinction demonstrates what decades of coordinated conservation can achieve. Yet the species remains dependent on active management because the threats that contributed to its decline have not simply disappeared. USFWS plans to continue monitoring the fish after delisting, while conservation partners maintain barriers, control non-native trout and protect its remaining habitat. The agency plans post-delisting monitoring for at least 10 years.For Arizona’s native trout, the new Big Bonito Creek barrier is therefore more than another piece of infrastructure. It represents another layer of protection for a species that survived decades of pressure and now has a stronger foothold in the mountain streams where it evolved.

articles.title: RMIT researchers found a way to turn cigarette butts into bricks; adding 1% waste could cut brick-firing energy use by 10%
articles.summary: Experiments & Discoveries News: Cigarette butts are one of the world’s most common forms of litter, but the researchers have found a way to reuse this waste by incorporating it into .
articles.body: Cigarette butts are one of the world’s most common forms of litter, but the researchers have found a way to reuse this waste by incorporating it into bricks. Their research explores how discarded cigarette filters could be collected, processed, and added to lightweight fired-clay bricks on an industrial scale. Earlier RMIT research found that bricks containing 1% recycled cigarette butts could match the strength of conventional bricks while using less energy during production. The researchers also examined the health and safety concerns involved in handling cigarette waste, including harmful bacteria and heavy metals. The approach could therefore help reduce cigarette butt litter while also lowering the energy required to produce bricks.How cigarette waste could be used to make lightweight bricksRMIT researchers developed a plan to recycle cigarette butts into bricks on a larger scale. The approach builds on earlier work showing that fired-clay bricks containing 1% recycled cigarette butts can be as strong as conventional bricks. The latest plan outlines how the brickmaking and waste management industries could work together to collect discarded filters and use them in brick production. Researchers examined several ways to add the material, including whole cigarette butts, shredded filters, or a pre-mix combined with other brickmaking ingredients. The plan also includes health and safety measures for both industrial production and handmade bricks to address the risks associated with handling cigarette waste.What makes discarded cigarette butts harmful to the environmentCigarette butts contain toxic substances that can remain in the environment for years after they are discarded. According to RMIT, cigarette filters contain more than 60 chemicals known to cause cancer, along with heavy metals such as arsenic, chromium, nickel and cadmium. When cigarette butts are left as litter, these substances can make their way into soil and waterways.The research also examines bacteria found on discarded filters and how heavy metals can enter the environment.“Firing butts into bricks is a reliable and practical way to deal with this terrible environmental problem, while at the same time cutting brickmaking production costs,” says lead researcher Abbas Mohajerani. This could help prevent these contaminants from spreading into streets, soil, rivers and waterways.Recycled cigarette waste could offer benefits beyond waste reductionCigarette butts could serve a useful purpose during brick production rather than simply being sealed inside the finished product. RMIT research found that replacing 1% of the brick material with cigarette butts could reduce the energy needed for firing by 10%. Brick firing can take up to 30 hours, so cutting the energy needed for this process could make manufacturing more efficient.The researchers also found that bricks containing cigarette butts are lighter and offer better insulation than conventional bricks. These characteristics could help lower heating and cooling needs in buildings. The recycled material could offer benefits during manufacturing and throughout the life of the finished bricks.How much cigarette waste could be used in brick productionThe sheer volume of cigarette waste makes collection an important part of the proposed recycling system. RMIT reports that more than 6 trillion cigarettes are produced worldwide each year, generating about 1.2 million tonnes of toxic waste. The researchers note that specialised bins could help local authorities collect discarded cigarette butts before they become litter and make the material easier for brickmakers to access.Their analysis found that using cigarette butts in just 2.5% of global brick production, at a rate of 1%, would match the number of cigarettes produced each year. A reliable collection system would be essential to supply enough discarded butts for recycling.What measures could help reduce cigarette butt litterThe researchers say recycling technology alone will not be enough to tackle cigarette butt litter. Their plan also calls for stronger laws, tougher penalties for littering and specialised collection bins. These measures could help keep cigarette butts out of streets, rivers and oceans while creating a steady supply of waste for recycling. The team proposes dedicated recycling facilities linked to brickmaking in countries around the world.Such facilities could connect waste collection with brick production and make the process easier to manage on a larger scale. The researchers believe that combining recycling technology with organised collection systems and stronger anti-littering measures could help reduce cigarette waste and its impact on the environment.
